analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to give rebates on medicines sold to federally funded community health and family planning clinics.
analysis.headline: The Senate health committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in March 1992, but it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required drug manufacturers to pay rebates when they sell prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, and birth control devices to clinics that receive federal health funding — community health centers, migrant health centers, family planning projects, AIDS treatment entities, black lung clinics, and sexually transmitted disease clinics. The rebate would equal the difference between what the clinic paid and the lower of the negotiated price or the Medicaid price. Grants to the clinics could not be reduced because they received rebates, and clinics could not resell the discounted drugs. A later committee version replaced mandatory rebates with negotiated discount agreements and added a waiver and dispute-resolution process.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income patients who get care at federally funded community health centers, migrant clinics, family planning projects, and similar safety-net clinics would pay less for prescriptions, vaccines, and birth control. The clinics themselves would stretch their federal grants further, since rebates could not reduce their grant amounts.

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to pay covered clinics a rebate equal to the gap between the clinic's purchase price and the lower of the negotiated price or the Medicaid price, covering prescription drugs, over-the-counter drugs, and birth control devices.
Covers a broad set of safety-net providers, including community health centers, migrant health centers, family planning projects, AIDS-related service entities, black lung clinics, and STD clinics.
Bars any reduction in the clinics' federal grants as a result of the rebates, so the savings stay with the clinics rather than being clawed back by the government.
Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate contracts on behalf of the clinics aimed at holding prices at or below their September 1990 levels, adjusted for inflation.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, which would pay the rebates or provide the discounts. To the extent manufacturers could not recoup that cost elsewhere, it would come out of their revenue on sales to these clinics.

drawbacks.text: The rebate program is administratively heavy: clinics must submit quarterly claims on units purchased and average prices paid, and the Secretary must consolidate and process those claims — a burden for small clinics, which is why the bill allows some clinics to file claims on a consolidated state or project basis.
The bill prohibits clinics from reselling any discounted drug, with a $25,000 civil penalty per violation, to keep discounted product out of the resale market.

The committee-substitute version softened the original mandate: mandatory rebates became negotiated discount agreements with a maximum discount limit, manufacturers providing discounts could not also be forced to pay rebates under Medicaid or other government programs, and the whole scheme could be waived if participation was comparable to the Medicaid rebate program's — concessions that reduced the savings clinics would get.

A good-faith concern with mandatory discounts is that manufacturers may recoup the cost through higher prices elsewhere in the system; the bill required a Secretary's report on savings achieved and administrative costs, acknowledging this had to be measured.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered real, targeted savings — cheaper drugs and birth control for patients at safety-net clinics, and stretched grant dollars for the clinics — at the cost of manufacturer revenue and some administrative complexity. The committee substitute already traded away the strongest version (automatic Medicaid-style rebates) for negotiated discounts with caps and a waiver, so the final design was modest and cautious rather than aggressive.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate health committee approved the bill with an amendment and put it on the Senate's calendar of pending business, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Kennedy introduced the bill in September 1991 and it was referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources, which held hearings in October 1991.
On February 5, 1992, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and it was reported to the Senate on March 3, 1992 with written report 102-259.

The committee substitute changed the original design from mandatory rebates to negotiated discount agreements, added a maximum discount limit, a prime vendor distribution program, a certification process for covered entities, an anti-double-dipping provision, and a waiver.

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 414) on March 3, 1992, where it remained; no floor vote occurred before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off because the bill died: they avoided mandatory rebates or discounts on sales to federally funded community health centers, family planning clinics, and other safety-net providers, and low-income clinic patients never received the lower prices.

for.what_they_did: Held hearings, then ordered and reported the bill favorably to the Senate with a substitute amendment.

against.what_they_did: Opposed government-mandated price concessions; the committee substitute's shift from automatic rebates to negotiated discounts with caps and a waiver reflects the pushback such mandates drew.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all nine cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill cleared the Democratic-led Senate committee, but no floor vote was ever held, so no recorded partisan vote positions exist.

industries.note: The bill would have forced drug makers to pay rebates or grant discounts on every sale to federally funded safety-net clinics, benchmarked against Medicaid pricing. Their revenue on those sales would fall, which is exactly the cost that low-income clinic patients' savings would come from.

The reported version required a bid process to establish a prime vendor program under which covered entities pay wholesalers for distribution and related services to facilitate discounted purchases — a new, guaranteed channel of distribution business.
